Take the real 14-stock basket, Gaussianize each marginal, and rank every pair by
mutual information.  The deliverable is an **MI ranking** that catches dependence
correlation alone would miss.

---

## 1 · Load and Gaussianize the Marginals

::: {#f7d86fa4 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R = datasets.load_returns()
META = datasets.load_basket_meta()
label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"]))
tickers = list(R.columns)

G = {t: gaussianize_1d(R[t].to_numpy()) for t in tickers}   # normal scores
print(f"{len(R)} days × {len(tickers)} stocks, marginals Gaussianized")
print("example — JPM normal scores: mean "
      f"{G['JPM'].mean():+.2f}, std {G['JPM'].std():.2f}")
```

## 2 · Rank Every Pair by Mutual Information

::: {#196b2b46 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rows = []
for u, v in itertools.combinations(tickers, 2):
    mi = mutual_information_xy(G[u], G[v], bins=16)
    rho = np.corrcoef(R[u], R[v])[0, 1]
    rows.append((f"{u}/{v}", rho, mi))
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[2], reverse=True)

print(f"{'pair':<10}{'Pearson':>9}{'MI (nats)':>11}")
print("-" * 30)
for pair, rho, mi in rows[:10]:
    print(f"{pair:<10}{rho:>+9.2f}{mi:>11.3f}")
```
